title: Pecan and the Moon Pebble
markdown:
In a cozy oak whose leaves felt like green blankets, the kind that make a squirrel want to snuggle, lived Pecan. He was not just any squirrel. His tail twitched and jiggled with excitement, as if it had its own little happy dance, and his eyes sparkled the way treasures do when they have just been found. Every day, without fail, he scampered and scurried the forest floor. His paws went tap-tap-tap. His nose twitched. He hunted anything that winked or gleamed or shimmered.

A spiderweb beaded with dew looked like a necklace of a million tiny diamonds. A scrap of sunshine caught on a leaf glowed like a lamp small enough for a pocket. “Ooh, shiny,” he would chatter, and then he would tuck it carefully into his super-cozy nest among the other winks and gleams.

Nearby drifted Halo, a halo moth whose wings were soft glowing moonbeams. Halo did not collect. Halo was a light. When the big bright sun tucked itself behind the hills and the shy stars began to peek, Halo moved through the sleepy trees like a warm fuzzy hug. He helped lost beetles find their way home to their mamas and papas. He made the shy night flowers glow a little brighter, as if they were whispering secrets to the moon. Pecan and Halo were the closest of friends, and they loved the quiet forest more than any pile of sparkle.

One afternoon Pecan dug near a brook that sang a happy shush-shush song, as if it were telling secrets to its pebbles. His little paws hit something hard. He pulled it out, and his eyes went as wide as two saucers. It was not only shiny. It was moon-shiny. A pebble, all smooth and round, that held the same light as a sleepy moon peeking through clouds.

“This is the mooniest thing I have ever seen.”

He held it up to his nose. A small flutter started in his tummy, a flutterbug doing cartwheels. Not a bad flutter. A tiny feeling that this special moon-pebble did not belong in the nest with the dewdrops and the captured sun. It belonged somewhere else, somewhere even more particular.

For a moment he almost tucked it into the nest anyway. The other shinies would have made room. The pebble sat in his paws and kept being moonlight, and the nest suddenly felt like the wrong kind of dark. He knew exactly who to ask. He clutched the pebble and scampered up the tall oak as fast as his legs could carry him, pausing once on a branch to look at it again, just to be sure the glow had not been a trick of the brook. He found Halo drifting past, light twinkling like a friendly sleepy wink.

“Halo. Look what I found. A moon-pebble. I think it needs to go back to the Moon Pond.”

Halo’s antennae wiggled with curiosity. His voice was like the rustle of dry leaves.

“The Moon Pond. That sounds like the right kind of special. I can help, Pecan. Let’s go.”

They set off on a gentle quiet journey. They had to tiptoe extra carefully past a clutch of sleepy baby birds. Halo’s light found the quiet path. The forest was so still. The only sounds were the soft thump of Pecan’s paws on moss and the whoosh of Halo’s wings, no louder than breath. They floated past flowers with petals curled tight like tiny sleeping babies dreaming sweet dreams. They passed a family of hedgehogs tucked snug into a pile of crunchy leaves. Everything was peaceful. Pecan felt a happy hum buzzing in his tummy, like a bumblebee that had decided not to hurry.

The path narrowed where ferns leaned together. Halo dimmed his light so the sleeping things would stay sleeping, then brightened it again when the moss grew dark. Pecan held the pebble close to his chest. It felt cooler than the other treasures, as if it remembered being sky.

At the edge of a big open clearing the Moon Pond waited. It was not a splashy noisy pond. It was small and perfectly still, a looking glass that held the moon exactly. Tiny silver sparkles danced on the water like fairy lights that had forgotten to go home. Pecan took a deep breath. He walked slowly to the rim. His paws sank a little into the soft moonlit grass.

He flicked his wrist. The pebble tumbled in.

Plink.

The softest sweetest note. The pebble’s smooth surface caught the moonlight and sent silvery ripples across the still water, then sank with a slow graceful descent, a cool whisper against glass. At the bottom it did not vanish. It began to gleam, a soft steady light, like a tiny happy star that had found the right floor.

Pecan and Halo watched until the ripples settled. Their hearts felt full and calm, like a warm bath. The pebble looked as if it had been waiting for that exact dark.

Pecan still collected sparkly things after that. He still found treasures that gleamed like captured sunshine. He did not say the most special things in the whole wide world belong to special places. He only glanced once more at the star on the pond floor, then followed Halo’s soft light home through the trees, his empty paws lighter than any nestful of shine.
